hints: Picture the two directions you know - the electron velocity into the slice and the magnetic field B across the slice - and remember you need a direction perpendicular to both for the force.
walkthrough:
**Sort out velocity and field directions**
Think of the electrons entering face PQKJ and moving straight into the slice, while the field $B$ points horizontally across the slice. The magnetic force must be at right angles to both.

**Apply Fleming's left-hand rule carefully**
For negative electrons, the conventional current is opposite to the electron motion. Using $F = Bqv$ with the left hand gives a force directed vertically downwards, toward the bottom of the slice.
Final answer: Downwards, perpendicular to both $v$ and $B$.

hints: If the magnetic force pushes all the free electrons toward one side, which pair of opposite faces will gain excess electrons and which will be left positive?
walkthrough:
**Follow where the electrons pile up**
The downward magnetic force in (a)(i) drives electrons to the bottom face. That face becomes negative while the opposite top face is left positive.

**Name the faces**
From Fig. 8.1 the top face is PQRS and the bottom face is JKLM. The Hall p.d. therefore develops between face PQRS and face JKLM.
Final answer: Face PQRS and face JKLM, i.e. the top and bottom faces.

hints: Think about the separation of charge: as electrons are deflected to one face, an electric field develops across the slice.
In the steady state, the electric force on an electron balances the magnetic force, preventing further charge accumulation.
walkthrough:
**Charge separation creates an electric field**
As electrons accumulate on one face, that face becomes negative and the opposite face positive. This is like a parallel-plate capacitor, so a transverse electric field $E$ builds up across the slice.

**A new opposing force appears**
Any further electron moving through now feels an electric force: $$F_E = eE$$ This acts upwards, opposite to the downward magnetic force: $$F_B = Bev$$

**Equilibrium gives maximum p.d.**
As more charge piles up, $E$ and $F_E$ grow. Very quickly: $$eE = Bev$$ The net transverse force becomes zero, electrons stop being deflected, and the p.d. $V_H$ across the faces stops increasing at its maximum value.

Final answer: Separated charge sets up a transverse electric field E across the slice. This exerts an electric force $eE$ on electrons opposite to the magnetic force $Bev$. When $eE = Bev$ no further deflection occurs, so the Hall p.d. $V_H = Ed$ reaches a steady maximum.

hints: Use the Hall voltage formula $V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$, identifying which dimension represents the thickness $t$ parallel to the magnetic field.
Substitute $B$, $I$, $n$, elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, and $t$ in metres to calculate the Hall voltage.
walkthrough:
**Write the Hall equation**
At equilibrium $V_H$ is given by: $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ where $t$ is the thickness PQ $= 0.10 \text{ mm}$, $n = 1.3 \times 10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$, $B = 4.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$, $I = 6.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ A}$ and $q = e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

**Substitute and calculate**
$$V_H = \frac{(4.6 \times 10^{-3})(6.3 \times 10^{-4})}{(1.3 \times 10^{29})(1.0 \times 10^{-4})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}$$ $$V_H = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{-6}}{2.08 \times 10^{6}} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-12} \text{ V}$$ This is the steady transverse p.d. across the slice.

hints: Note that the Hall voltage in a metal is of the order of $10^{-12}\text{ V}$, which is extremely difficult to measure.
Semiconductors have a much lower charge carrier density $n$, and since $V_H \propto \frac{1}{n}$, the resulting Hall voltage is much larger and easier to measure.
walkthrough:
**Judge the metal result**
In (c) $V_H \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-12} \text{ V}$. That is picovolt level, far too tiny to measure reliably with ordinary voltmeters and easily lost in noise.

**Compare carrier densities**
A metal has a huge free-electron density $n \sim 10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$. A semiconductor has a much smaller $n$, by many orders of magnitude, because only few charge carriers are available.

**Link to Hall sensitivity**
Since: $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq} \propto \frac{1}{n}$$ a smaller $n$ gives a much larger $V_H$ for the same $B$, $I$ and $t$. Semiconductors therefore give a large, measurable Hall voltage and make practical, sensitive Hall probes.

Final answer: Metals have very large $n$, giving $V_H \approx 10^{-12} \text{ V}$ which is too small to measure. Semiconductors have much smaller $n$, so $V_H = BI/ntq$ is much larger and easily measurable, making a more sensitive Hall probe.
